items.title: 12.3.3 Continuity of a Function at a Point

blocks.text:
A function \(f\) is said to be continuous at a number "\(c\)" if and only if the following three conditions are satisfied.

(i) \(f(c)\) is defined
(ii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists
(iii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What each condition guards against:
(i) \(f(c)\) defined: there must be a point of the graph at \(x = c\) (no hole).
(ii) the limit exists: the left and right parts of the graph must head for the same height (no jump).
(iii) limit \(= f(c)\): the point at \(x = c\) must sit exactly where the curve is heading (no point out of place).
In short, continuity at \(c\) means you can draw the graph through \(x = c\) without lifting your pencil.
If one or more of these three conditions fail to hold at "\(c\)", then the function \(f\) is said to be discontinuous at "\(c\)".

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Working order for any question: test (i), then (ii), then (iii). Stop at the first condition that fails and say which one failed. If all three hold, the function is continuous.
For a polynomial (like Example 12) all three conditions always hold at every real \(c\), because the limit is found by substitution, which gives exactly \(f(c)\).

blocks.title: Example 11
blocks.problem: Consider the function \(f(x) = \frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1}\), discuss the continuity of \(f\) at \(x = 1\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1}\).
To find: whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 1\).
Method: test the three conditions of continuity in order; as soon as one fails, \(f\) is discontinuous.

Step 1: Condition (i), is \(f(1)\) defined?
\[f(1) = \dfrac{1^{2}-1}{1-1} = \dfrac{0}{0}\]
Why: \(\frac{0}{0}\) is not a number (division by zero is not defined), so \(f(1)\) is not defined.

Step 2: Conclusion
Condition (i) fails, so \(f(x)\) is discontinuous at \(x = 1\).
Why: continuity needs all three conditions; one failure is enough for discontinuity.

Check: the limit itself does exist,
\[\lim_{x \to 1} \dfrac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1} = \lim_{x \to 1}(x+1)\]
\[= 2\]
but there is no point of the graph at \(x = 1\): the graph is the line \(y = x + 1\) with a hole at \((1, 2)\). So the function is still discontinuous.
blocks.answer: \(f(1)\) is not defined, so \(f(x)\) is discontinuous at \(x = 1\).

blocks.title: Example 12
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 3x^{2} - 5x + 4\).
To find: whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 1\).
Method: find \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)\) and \(f(1)\) and compare (conditions (i)-(iii)).

Step 1: The limit
\[\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1} (3x^{2} - 5x + 4)\]
\[= 3 - 5 + 4 = 2\]
Why: \(f\) is a polynomial, so by the theorems on limits its limit is found by substituting \(x = 1\): \(3(1)^{2} - 5(1) + 4\). The limit exists: condition (ii).

Step 2: The value
\[f(1) = 3 - 5 + 4 = 2\]
Why: \(f(1)\) is a real number, so condition (i) holds.

Step 3: Compare
\[\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = f(1) = 2\]
Therefore \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x = 1\).
Why: all three conditions hold; (iii) is the equality of the limit and the value.

Check: values near 1 are near 2:
\[f(0.99) = 1.9903,\quad f(1.01) = 2.0103\]
blocks.answer: \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = f(1) = 2\), so \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x = 1\).

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem:
Discuss the continuity of the functions \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) at \(x = 3\)
(a) \[f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3} & \text{if } x \ne 3 \\ 6 & \text{if } x = 3 \end{cases}\]
(b) \[g(x) = \dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3} \ \text{ if } x \ne 3\]
steps:
Given: \(f\) and \(g\) above; both equal \(\frac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}\) for \(x \ne 3\), but \(f(3) = 6\) while \(g\) has no value at 3.
To find: whether \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous at \(x = 3\).
Method: check the three conditions; to find the limit, factorise \(x^{2} - 9\) and cancel \(x - 3\) (the \(\frac{0}{0}\) form).

(a) Step 1: Condition (i)
\[f(3) = 6\]
Why: the second line of the definition gives the value at \(x = 3\) directly.

(a) Step 2: Condition (ii), the limit
\[\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}\]
\[= \lim_{x \to 3} \dfrac{(x+3)(x-3)}{x-3}\]
\[= \lim_{x \to 3} (x+3)\]
\[= 3 + 3 = 6\]
Why: near 3 (but \(x \ne 3\)) the first formula is used. Direct substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\), so we use \(x^{2} - 9 = (x+3)(x-3)\) and cancel \(x - 3\), which is allowed because \(x \ne 3\) while \(x \to 3\).

(a) Step 3: Condition (iii)
\[\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = 6 = f(3)\]
So \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x = 3\). There is no break in the graph.
Why: all three conditions hold.

(b) Step 4: Condition (i) for \(g\)
\(g\) is not defined at \(x = 3\) (its only formula is for \(x \ne 3\)).
\(\Rightarrow g(x)\) is discontinuous at \(x = 3\).
Why: condition (i) fails. The limit is still 6 (same working as in (a)), but there is no point \((3, g(3))\), so the graph has a break (a hole) at \(x = 3\).

Check: for \(x \ne 3\) both functions equal \(x + 3\); e.g.
\[f(2) = \dfrac{4-9}{2-3} = 5 = 2 + 3\]
The graphs are the line \(y = x + 3\); \(f\) fills the point \((3, 6)\), \(g\) leaves it empty.
blocks.answer: (a) \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x = 3\) (\(\lim_{x \to 3} f(x) = 6 = f(3)\)). (b) \(g(x)\) is discontinuous at \(x = 3\) (\(g(3)\) is not defined).

blocks.caption: Figure: Example 13(a), graph of f, no break at x = 3 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of g on axes x and y: the straight line y = x + 3 through the filled points (0, 3), (2, 5) and (4, 7), with an open circle (a hole) at (3, 6) because g is not defined at x = 3; a dashed vertical line drops from the hole to x = 3 on the x-axis.
blocks.caption: Figure: Example 13(b), graph of g, a hole at (3, 6) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the book's graph for Example 13(b), the point \((3, 6)\) is drawn as a solid dot on an unbroken line, although \(g\) is not defined at \(x = 3\) and the text says there is a break in the graph there. The point \((3, 6)\) must be an open circle (a hole), as in our drawing.

blocks.title: Example 14
blocks.problem:
Discuss continuity of \(f(x)\) at \(x = 3\), when
\[f(x) = \begin{cases} x - 1, & \text{if } x < 3 \\ 2x + 1, & \text{if } 3 \le x \end{cases}\]
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x - 1\) for \(x < 3\) and \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) for \(x \ge 3\).
To find: whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 3\).
Method: \(x = 3\) is where the formula changes, so check \(f(3)\), then the left and right hand limits (criterion 12.3.2), then compare.

Step 1: Condition (i)
\[f(3) = 2(3) + 1 = 7\]
Condition (i) is satisfied.
Why: \(x = 3\) satisfies \(3 \le x\), so the second formula gives the value.

Step 2: Left hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 3^{-}} (x - 1)\]
\[= 3 - 1 = 2\]
Why: for \(x < 3\) the first formula applies.

Step 3: Right hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to 3^{+}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 3^{+}} (2x + 1)\]
\[= 6 + 1 = 7\]
Why: for \(x > 3\) the second formula applies.

Step 4: Condition (ii)
\[\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} f(x) \ne \lim_{x \to 3^{+}} f(x)\]
i.e., condition (ii) is not satisfied: \(\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\) does not exist.
Hence \(f(x)\) is not continuous at \(x = 3\).
Why: \(2 \ne 7\); by the criterion of 12.3.2 the limit does not exist, and without a limit condition (ii) fails.
Check: the graph (below) jumps at \(x = 3\) from height 2 (left piece, open end) to height 7 (right piece, filled end), e.g. \(f(2.99) = 1.99\) and \(f(3.01) = 7.02\).
blocks.answer: The left hand limit is 2 and the right hand limit is 7, so \(\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)\) does not exist; \(f(x)\) is not continuous at \(x = 3\).

blocks.alt: Graph of f on axes x and y: the line y = x minus 1 for x less than 3, crossing the axes at (1, 0) and (0, minus 1) and ending at an open circle at (3, 2); the line y = 2x + 1 for x at least 3, starting at a filled dot at (3, 7). Dashed lines join (3, 2) and (3, 7) to the y-axis at 2 and 7 and to x = 3 on the x-axis.
blocks.caption: Figure: Example 14, a jump at x = 3 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's solution calls the graph "figure (iii)", but the figure carries no number. In that graph the end of the left piece at \((3, 2)\) is drawn as a solid dot; since \(f(3) = 7\), the point \((3, 2)\) is not on the graph and must be an open circle, as in our drawing. The solid dot belongs at \((3, 7)\) only.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Write the three conditions in your answer with a tick or a cross: "(i) \(f(3) = 7\) defined; (ii) LHL \(= 2\), RHL \(= 7\), limit does not exist; hence discontinuous." A clear statement of which condition fails earns full marks.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) if and only if (i) \(f(c)\) is defined, (ii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists, (iii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)\).
2. If any one condition fails, \(f\) is discontinuous at \(c\).
3. Three kinds of break: a hole (Examples 11, 13(b)), a jump (Example 14), a point out of place (limit exists but \(\ne f(c)\)).
4. A polynomial is continuous at every real number.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Saying "the limit exists, so \(f\) is continuous": in Example 11 the limit is 2 but \(f(1)\) is not defined.
2. Saying "\(f(c)\) is defined, so \(f\) is continuous": in Example 14 \(f(3) = 7\) but the limit does not exist.
3. Cancelling \(x - 3\) and then putting \(x = 3\) into the original fraction to find \(f(3)\); \(f(3)\) comes only from the definition of the function.
